overview: Medieval Novgorod was a powerful trading city and the centre of a large northern territory. Its republican institutions developed gradually, with an influential aristocratic elite. The map covers 1200 to 1492; those dates do not describe the republic’s exact lifespan.

periods.title: Republican institutions take shape
periods.summary: The expulsion of a prince in 1136 is a conventional turning point, within a longer development of autonomous government.

periods.title: A northern trading power
periods.summary: Novgorod’s commercial relationships and political institutions connected the city with a wide northern territory and the Baltic.

periods.title: Under Muscovite rule
periods.summary: Muscovite conquest ended the republic’s autonomy in 1478. The city and its communities continued under changed political authority.

sections.title: Government and people from far away

items.text: The assembly known as the veche was part of Novgorod’s political life, but this was not a modern democracy with equal votes for everybody. Historian Pavel Lukin emphasizes the power of local aristocratic families, the boyars. Public ideas of brotherhood coexisted with unequal influence.

Foreign merchants had permanent trading courts in the city. Traders from Gotland established one, while German merchants developed St Peter’s Court. Furs and wax were important exports. Novgorod belonged to a commercial network that also connected places such as Bergen, London and Bruges.

sections.title: A city preserved in wet ground

items.text: Novgorod’s marshy ground made wooden street surfaces useful. Layers of clay kept the soil wet, helping preserve wood and leather that would usually decay. Archaeologists can therefore study ordinary belongings as well as the stone churches that remained above ground.

Leather shoes, comb cases, knife sheaths and toys survived in these waterlogged layers. Wooden and leather playthings offer a view of childhood beyond famous princes and battles. A lost toy can tell a historian something that a royal chronicle never thought to mention.

Leather masks from a cobbler’s workshop may have been worn by children, or during folk celebrations. Their exact use remains uncertain. We have the masks, but not the invitation explaining who was supposed to wear them.

sections.title: Homework, doodles and a marriage proposal

items.text: Many Novgorod notes were scratched into birch bark with a pointed tool instead of written in ink. Surviving examples concern debts, taxes and orders for icons. Writing could help arrange ordinary business as well as preserve religious texts. These finds do not establish that every resident could read.

A boy named Onfim practised letters and syllables in the mid-thirteenth century, then drew warriors and a horseman. The museum estimates he was about six or seven from his drawings; his exact age is unknown. Apparently homework and action scenes already competed for attention.

Onfim labelled one creature “ѧ звѣре”, meaning “I am a beast.” This Old East Slavic phrase appears in Cyrillic on birch-bark document 199, dated about 1240 to 1260. The scholarly transcription separates the words. It is a real child’s caption, not a modern imitation of medieval speech.

A later birch-bark fragment records Mikita proposing marriage to Malanija and naming a witness. The catalogue places it around 1280 to 1300, possibly earlier. The message reveals one person’s direct approach to marriage; it cannot tell us how every family arranged a wedding.

Thirteenth-century material excavated near Borkova Street contained waste that researchers believe had been moved from a cesspit. Five samples revealed raspberry, currant, strawberry, cranberry and other fruit remains. This small, redeposited sample offers clues to food, but cannot supply a menu for the whole city.

The same samples contained seeds of herbs including mint, catmint and oregano. The researchers suggest possible use in drinks or medicinal mixtures. That remains an interpretation: finding a seed does not reveal the exact recipe, the ailment being treated or whether any remedy worked.

A research project that sieved Novgorod’s archaeological deposits recovered evidence that local fish, including pike and zander, were common food. Careful sieving matters because small bones can easily be missed. Changing how archaeologists collect evidence can change the picture of what people ate.

The mid-eleventh-century Cathedral of St Sophia predates this map record. Later churches include the Transfiguration church with fourteenth-century frescoes by Theophanes the Greek. Architecture and painting developed across several generations, leaving a cultural history much longer than any single map snapshot.

ending.text: Muscovite rulers conquered Novgorod in 1478, ending its autonomous republican government. People continued living in the city, and its churches, art and everyday traces survived across later centuries. The imported 1492 endpoint is a map-data boundary, not the date of that conquest.

sources.note: Fragment, conventionally 1280 to 1300 with possible earlier dating. Original and Schaeken translation name Malanija; older Kovalev English translation incorrectly says Anna.
